Off the Wire Press Releases

LineShine Supports Gordon Bell Finalist Work on Silicon and Battery Materials

Nov. 15, 2026 — Following the domestically developed LineShine supercomputer’s top rankings on both the June 2026 TOP500 and HPCG lists, Shenzhen’s independent innovation in supercomputing has once again gained international recognition. Earlier this year, the XLSDFT computing software independently developed by the team of Associate Researcher Qimen Xu, Associate Researcher Yu Zhang, Professor Haohuan Fu, and Professor Yutong Lu at the National Supercomputing Center in Shenzhen has been named a finalist for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The finalist selection project is titled “Extreme-Scale Linear-Scaling Kohn-Sham DFT at 100 Million Atoms: Bridging Quantum Simulations and Experiments.” This achievement propels Kohn-Sham density functional theory computation into the era of 100 million atoms: the peak performance of FP64 (double-precision floating-point) in the key computational stage reaches 1.31 EFlop/s, crossing the exascale application performance threshold.

Figure 1. XLSDFT enables quantum-mechanical simulations of all-solid-state battery interfaces at experimentally relevant scales.

The ACM Gordon Bell Prize is the highest international award in the field of high-performance computing applications. It annually recognizes outstanding achievements in solving major scientific and engineering problems using advanced parallel computing, focusing on performance, scalability, solution efficiency, and scientific value. This nomination extends Shenzhen Supercomputing’s independent innovation achievements beyond its world-leading exascale computing system to include original algorithms, independently developed application software, and cutting-edge scientific discoveries.

Scaling DFT to 200 Million Atoms

XLSDFT breaks through a scale bottleneck that has constrained quantum simulation of materials for decades. Density functional theory (DFT) can predict the electronic structure and properties of materials from a quantum mechanical perspective and is the core method for materials computation; however, the computational complexity of traditional Kohn-Sham DFT typically increases cubically with the number of atoms and the memory requirement increases quadratically, limiting its practical applications to hundreds to thousands of atoms and making it difficult to reach defects, interfaces, and reaction layers in real materials. The Shenzhen supercomputing team has proposed the XLSDFT framework, which, through algorithmic innovations such as divide-and-conquer density matrices and Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration, simultaneously reduces computational and memory complexity to linear scaling, pushing the computable scale from “thousands of atoms” to “hundreds of millions of atoms” while maintaining the accuracy of Kohn-Sham DFT.

Silicon and Battery Interface Results

This work sets two Kohn-Sham DFT world records. First, XLSDFT achieved a system scaling test of 100 million atoms on 20,480 LineShine computing nodes, with a weak-scaling efficiency of 96.6%, and successfully completed calculations on a 200 million-atom silicon system, increasing the computable scale to 20 times the previous record of 10 million atoms. Second, the team performed DFT calculations on an interface between lithium metal and the sulfide solid electrolyte LGPS containing approximately 11.33 million atoms, reaching a scale relevant to experimental characterization and about 1,000 times that of previous studies of similar complex interfaces.

Connecting Simulations and Experiments

For a long time, a significant scale gap has existed between digital simulation and physical experiments: traditional Kohn-Sham DFT can typically only handle hundreds to thousands of atoms, making it difficult to construct complex interface models sufficient to correspond to the experimental characterization range. As the number of atoms increases from thousands to tens of millions, the computational cost for traditional algorithms, which typically increase cubically with the number of atoms, drastically increases, making it difficult to directly and quantitatively compare computational results with experimental measurements for a long time. This study, targeting the lithium metal-LGPS interface with approximately 11.33 million atoms, used DeepMD machine learning molecular dynamics to generate a realistic-scale interface structure, and then used XLSDFT to calculate the electronic structure. The results show a quantitative agreement with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) experiments on the trend of changes from the interface into the bulk material. This work partially bridges the long-standing scale gap between digital simulation and physical experiments, achieving direct comparison and mutual verification between digital and physical experiments on this representative interface system, and providing atomic-scale basis for the design of all-solid-state battery interfaces.

Hardware and Software Optimization

Crossing the exascale application performance threshold, this achievement stems from deep collaboration between algorithms, software, and computer systems. LineShine pioneered an architecture it calls ‘online acceleration,’ employing entirely domestically produced hardware and software, and comprises over 20,000 computing nodes. Each node is equipped with two domestically produced LX2 high-performance processors, along with on-package high-bandwidth memory and the LingQi high-speed interconnect network. The LX2 processor integrates SME and SVE computing units, enabling matrix acceleration directly within the CPU, reducing the overhead of migrating data to external accelerators. The team conducted system-level optimizations around the key computational and communication aspects of XLSDFT, allowing the original algorithm to fully unleash its performance on a domestically produced exascale supercomputing platform.

From LINPACK to Scientific Applications

The LineShine system boasts a theoretical peak performance of 2.736 EFlop/s, achieving 2.198 EFlop/s in the high-performance LINPACK (HPL) double-precision benchmark test, with a LINPACK efficiency of approximately 80.4%, ranking first in the TOP500 world. It also ranks first in HPCG, second in the June 2026 Graph500 breadth-first search ranking, and fourth in HPL-MxP. For real-world DFT scientific applications, XLSDFT completed a 100 million-atom test on 20,480 nodes, achieving a weak-scaling efficiency of 96.6%. During critical computational phases, the FP64 (double-precision floating-point) peak performance reached 1.31 EFlop/s, approximately 53% of the theoretical peak performance of the computational resources used. This demonstrates that LineShine’s exascale computing power is not only reflected in overall benchmark tests but has also been efficiently released during critical computational phases of major scientific applications. Machine learning molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations are both performed on this CPU-onlu system, collectively forming a new path for scientific computing that integrates HPC and AI. Currently, Shenzhen Supercomputing Center has used the platform for more than 10 applications combining HPC and AI, promoting advanced computing power to serve scientific research in different fields.

From Supercomputing to Scientific Discovery

From ranking first in both the TOP500 and HPCG lists to having its independently developed software named a finalist for the Gordon Bell Prize, Shenzhen Supercomputing Center is forming a complete innovation chain from independent systems and software to major scientific applications. This selection reflects the center’s continuous investment in recent years in attracting high-level talent, innovating original algorithms, integrating supercomputing and intelligent computing, and collaborative software and hardware R&D. Leveraging Shenzhen’s innovative ecosystem in fields such as artificial intelligence, new energy, new materials, and semiconductors, Shenzhen Supercomputing Center will further promote its independently developed software, such as XLSDFT, to more cutting-edge scientific and industrial applications, enabling world-leading computing power to be transformed into scientific discovery and technological innovation capabilities more quickly.

Editor’s note: This announcement was translated from Chinese and edited by HPCwire for clarity.

Source: National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS)
